utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Perisic. Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution with Ms. Bronagh McKenna and Ms. Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and everybody else in these proceedings. Mr. Perisic will be represented today by Tina Drolec, Milos Androvic, Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, Daniela Tasic, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution calls Mr. Morten Torkildsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we are waiting, early this morning I noticed another mistake that I had made in converting Milosevic 65 ter numbers to Perisic 65 ter numbers, and it's simply that at paragraph 66, page 23 of the report, there's a reference to 65 ter number 6550. It should say "65 ter number 6524."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please take the -- make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, before we begin, both you and I speak the English language, and we need just to be careful that we don't make life too difficult for the interpreters, and so I'd ask you to please try to perhaps pause between question and answer to give the interpreters a moment to catch up with us. If we don't do that, they will inform us. Is your name Morten Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you a citizen of Norway?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 9188, which will be the curriculum vitae of Mr. Torkildsen. Your Honours, I'm not seeing any evidence on my screen. I don't know if it's only my problem or it's -- here it comes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, this is a copy of your curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the second page, please, and maybe if we can make that a little bit bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your education was first a bachelor of science in management sciences at the University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And subsequently did you receive a master's degree?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, at the City University Business School.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was the focus of your master's degree?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Most of the focus of my master's degree was finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Torkildsen, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I'm a financial investigator, or by education I'm educated with two business degrees, but I've worked most of my working life as a financial investigator. Today I'm a partner in a law firm, being in charge of the financial investigations that we conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And briefly, what does a financial investigator do?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Basically he tries to identify the facts regarding certain allegations, and I -- well, in financial investigation, it's got very much to do with the documents, not as much as hearing witnesses. I would say that financial cases and investigations of those are 95 per cent based on what's contained within documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say that a financial investigator tries to identify the facts regarding certain allegations, can you be a little bit more specific? What kind of allegations do you work on?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Typically I work on allegations of fraud, corruption, and all kinds of financial irregularities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how long have you been doing this work?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I've been doing that for almost my whole working career, at least for the last 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you've done this work in Norway; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 1 -- back to page 1 of the curriculum, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just briefly, what kind of financial investigations have you done within Norway?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, it's not exactly like I conducted all of my investigations within Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, I know that, I'm speaking about within Norway right now.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I've done a lot of investigation into allegations of corruption and also a lot of kinds of fraud cases. I've been investigating corruption within the oil sector, the public sector in general, and typically also into the industry of building and construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, have you only done this kind of work, financial investigations, in Norway?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: No. Even most of my Norwegian cases had an international dimension.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: So one of the -- I'll give you one example, and that is one of the investigations I had out from Norway that involved actually conducting investigations in about 15 countries, both in Europe and in the US at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. At some point in your career, did you work for the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And briefly can you describe when that was and what you did.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That was exactly from the 2nd of January, 2001, until sometime in August 2003. I was a financial investigator, working for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would seek to tender 65 ter 9188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to having this CV of Mr. Torkildsen be admitted into evidence for one reason: This is his present CV, whereas he compiled his report in 2002 and then he attached the CV with that work of his which was linked to the period when he did his work. So what's relevant for us is whether, when he did the work, whether he had the necessary qualifications and not to assess his qualifications as of today in this present. Well, at least until I complete my cross-examination, I'd like this to be introduced and marked for identification only, until I complete my cross-examination, and then you can decide. Because attached to his report, we have received a CV from the period when he wrote it, when he did the work, which, in fact, was six years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand this last part, Mr. Lukic. You said: "Because attached to his report we have received a CV from the period when he wrote it, when he did the work, which, in fact, was six years ago." What does that sentence mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps I wasn't precise enough. The time that the paper was handed over, we received his CV as of then, which was rounded off and concluded with 2002, incorporated activities he was engaged in up until 2002 when he compiled the paper and did the work on it. So we cannot asses his competency on the basis of the experience he gained afterwards, post-2002, and that is provided in his present CV. Now, if the Prosecutor wants to tender into evidence his CV, he had a document -- he has a document attached to the paper dated 2002, his 2002 CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, when you look at this document that is on the screen now, which is the curriculum vitae of the witness, are you not able to see from that document what his qualifications and experience were as of 2002? Because, I mean, it gives his history from the time he qualified to date. And if you want to know what his competencies were in 2002, all you have to do is you look at from birth to 2002 in the current CV. He doesn't have to give you a CV of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think, Your Honour, that what we need with respect to assessing his qualifications is the CV that he gave then. That's the important one. I don't see why we should have a new CV if we've already got one from the previous period, because that's the relevant one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do have that one? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were provided it by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you do have one, that one, is your objection against the admission of the CV -- what are you asking for admission of?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I had asked for admission of the CV that you see on your screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- which is the most current curriculum vitae of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I see that the report that -- okay. We haven't been shown the report, but the report that has been handed over to the Trial Chamber is dated the 10th of October, 2008 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- well, I'm sorry, I don't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say what you want to say, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. However, the 10th of October, 2008 report substantively is exactly the same as the November 2002 report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much. Thank you very much for that. What I'm trying to say to you, Mr. Lukic, is if you look at the 2002 CV that you have, which we don't have, is it -- up to -- is this CV that's on the screen up to 2002, is it not the same as that one that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Let me just explain. Yes, that's right, they are. When you made your ruling on the adoption or calling Mr. Torkildsen to come into court, let me remind you, when you made that decision we had an objection with regard to some of his qualifications, and then you were focusing on that CV of his which was attached to his paper of 2002. Now, what I'd like to say is this: That CV, with respect to his activities up until 2002, in the period stipulated where he worked, what he did, and so on, it stipulates that in that previous CV, whereas this report we have the activities listed and not the periods. I think that the previous CV is far more useful as far as we're concerned because this present one incorporates details which we are not focusing on in the examination of this witness here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether that's a legal ground for objection, Mr. Lukic, because what I hear you saying in that last sentence is that you're now saying you want to give legal advice to the Prosecution on how they must conduct their trial; that they must use the 2002 CV instead of the current CV. They've chosen to use the CV, and I don't -- I don't think it is for the Trial Chamber to say, No, don't use this one; use the 2002. In their own wisdom, they decided this is the CV they want to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, it's up to them to decide how they're going to present their case. So I'll leave all these matters and have them cleared up during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think -- I was just going to suggest that, because if you say there are discrepancies between the 2002 CV and this CV, those are matters for cross-examination. Do you have any response to the objection, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then 65 ter 9188 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P309, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could now please bring up 65 ter number 6520.01 on the screen, which will be the report of Mr. Torkildsen, with the date of 10 October of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, this is the first page of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next page, in Roman numeral I, it says: "Outline of Task." Can you briefly describe to the Chamber, what were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Just to give a bit of background on that, and that is when I arrived at the Office of the Prosecutor in January 2001, the OTP as such, had collected documents for a period of close to eight years, and it was an enormous amount of documents contained within the evidence system of the OTP. And I was basically tasked to go through -- or actually, try to identify documents contained within the electronic evidence system of the OTP in order to try and determine whether there were any documents within that collection that could say anything about how the Serb-controlled districts in Croatia and Bosnia were financed by institutions allegedly controlled by Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And then, as you progressed in that, at some point were you given a task to do?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Again, as I said, my tasking was to try and identify the relevant documents talking about finance, and this was, of course, a huge task, so I used language personnel in order to assist me. And we did searchs in the electronic evidence system --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe my question wasn't clear because I think now you're really going into your methodology. Just with respect to this report, what were you asked to do? What were you asked to produce?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I was asked to produce financial evidence, if any, on how the Serb-controlled districts in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina was financed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, going back to methodology, which you describe briefly in paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 of your report, you mentioned that you conducted electronic searches.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did you conduct those searches?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Typically we were searching on specific key words, like "finance," "banking," "financial transfers," et cetera. And of course I was also provided with hard copies of quite a few documents. I mean, other members of the OTP had already been through parts of these large collections and also identified documents that I had to consider whether to be of relevance or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And at some point did you begin to analyse these documents in depth?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was sort of the second stage of this. I was trying to see whether there were any sort of pattern regarding how the financing took place. And in order to determine that, you had to sort of look at how documents relate to each other to be able to understand the broader picture of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And after you reviewed documents, either identified through electronic searches or hard-copy documents, in the OTP's possession, did you -- at some point did you select documents to use as references in your report?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I can just interrupt, how did you make this kind of selection?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, I sort of selected the documents that I thought was the most telling in terms of showing the pattern of the financial assistance that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to discuss a couple of translation issues, if I may, Mr. Torkildsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move, please, to page 22 of this report in the English version and pages 20 -- page 20 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I can just go back to your methodology for a moment. The documents that you selected, were they all strictly financial documents or were there other kinds of documents as well?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: No. They were typically -- well, most of them were official documents, typically military documents, but contained those -- within those military documents, there were information regarding finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask. Military documents of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of various armies. It could be the documents regarding the VRS. It was documents regarding the RSK army, documents originating from units within the Territorial Defence. There were documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Territorial Defence of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the Serb-controlled districts in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Also, documents regarding the JNA and later also the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, if you can turn your attention to paragraph 62 of your report --

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- you see here you are referring to a document. It's Prosecution 65 ter number 6530, a decision from the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the 14th of May, 1992. And you quote that document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there's a quote that you see there. It's one sentence long. And was that quote based on the English translation that you had available at the time?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please call up 65 ter 6530, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with 65 ter 20.01.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time could this report be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 6520.01 is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P310, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What are you now calling, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm calling up 65 ter 6530.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S version, if we could please move two pages further in, please, and the same with the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's page 12 in the B/C/S, at least I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There it is in the English. Yes, and if we could turn to page 12 of the B/C/S. I'm grateful to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There will be -- in the B/C/S there will be a number 187, as there is in the English version. Yes, that's now correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just focusing on the English version for now, it is a decision published in the "Official Gazette of the Serbian People" on the 8th of June, 1992. Is this the document that you quoted, Mr. Torkildsen, at paragraph 62?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This decision?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you take a look at Article 1 --

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- the document is entitled "Decision on the Use of Funds from Primary Issue." If you take a look at the first line of Article 1 --

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- and the very end of Article 2, you will notice that there are slight changes in the word order in the English in this most recent English translation.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do these changes in any way affect your conclusions, the conclusions of your report?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We could leave that document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you don't want to do anything with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, probably at this time, for the record, we should MFI it, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it be so MFIed and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P311, MFI, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And just one more translation issue. If we could go back to Mr. Torkildsen's report, which is MFI 310, and if we could turn to page 43 in the English version and page 41 of the B/C/S version, we'll focus on paragraph 118. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, if you look at paragraph 118, you see that you quote another document. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the document that you refer to is 65 ter 530. Mr. Torkildsen, at the time that you wrote your report and inserted these quotations, did you believe that you were quoting from a verbatim English translation of the original document?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two nights ago in my office, did you become aware that the translation that you used was not a verbatim English translation of the original?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could just, focusing on the first quote, which says: "From the beginning of the war, RS did not participate in financing of professional army members."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could ask Ms. Taseva's assistance again, could we please go to 65 ter 532, page 45 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want 532 or 523?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 532, Your Honour. As I said yesterday, the reference in the report to 523 was a typographical error by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we have the second English translation that is attached to 65 ter 530, please, and if we could go to page 40 at the bottom. No. I'm very sorry, Ms. Taseva, I believe the original translation that you selected was the correct one. We're looking for 0044 -- the ERN number 0044-7483, and I realise I'm breaking a rule by quoting the ERN number. Oh, yes, this is the correct page. Thank you. Can we focus on the bottom, please. I'm sorry, page 40, please, of the English, and focus on the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Here, Mr. Torkildsen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, just before you ask the question, and I notice Mr. Lukic, but -- just so that I follow you, you said at page 16, line 9 that you were calling 65 ter 532. At line 16, you said 530. What do we have here? Is it 530 or 532?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sincerely apologise. It is 65 -- it should be 530.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It should be 530.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Wait. I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's 532, and that is what we have on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for Colleague Saxon to find the page that he wished to find in English, but I can see that the B/C/S page does not correspond to the English page. So could we also find the relevant page in B/C/S on the screen prior to any questions being put.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It should be page 33 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that it, Mr. Lukic? Thank you. Okay, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, you'll notice in the second to the last paragraph, there is a sentence that says: "Republika Srpska has not taken part in financing the professional members of the army except for providing housing for several commanding officers." This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The third sentence of the penultimate paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So this is different from your first quotation at paragraph 118. Do you agree, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does the verbatim translation change your conclusions in any way?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: No. The substance is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we please move back again to marked for identification 310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this 532, you are not doing anything with it, the document on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't think that's necessary. I'm simply doing this for the basis of comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. But for purposes of the record, I would like to know, is it being -- do you want it marked? Are you not tendering it? What do you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we tender, then, page 40 of the English, Your Honour, and page 33 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 40 and 33 of the B/C/S -- page 40 of the English and 33 of the B/C/S of 65 ter 532 are admitted. And I say this is 65 ter 532 in the Milosevic case. It's not on your exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is on our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does this have a 65 ter number in your exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is that 532.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you. May it then be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we move on, could the first page of the document be included for context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The title page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, Madam Registrar, could they be included.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Page 1 and 30 of the English and page 1 and 33 of the B/C/S of 65 ter 532 will be Exhibit P312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 37 -- excuse me, could we move, please, to page 45 of the English and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of what, now? We're back at the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, if we're back at the report, could we please go to page 43 of the English and page 41 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, if you look at -- if you look at paragraph 118 again, your second quote, Mr. Torkildsen, it talks about how: "From 20 May 1992 to 31 August 1994, 1700 civilians received salaries from the SRY budget. From August 1994 these people have only been receiving allowance and no money has been paid to the pension fund. This is a task of the governments of SRJ and RS."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we please turn back to 65 ter 532, the prior translation that we were using, page 45 in the English version and page 37 in the B/C/S version. And if we could focus on the bottom of page 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Five lines from the bottom we see the following sentence: "After the departure of the former JNA, these persons, about 1700 of them, were awarded the salaries of workers in our army --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the status of workers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me. "... were awarded the status of workers in our army according to which they are entitled to all statutory powers and treatment according to other workers in the --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "Accorded."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "... and treatment accorded to other workers in Republika Srpska. From 20 May 1992 to 31 August 1994, they received their salaries through the FRY budget, and after that date they ..." Can we turn to the top of the next page, please. "... received only benefits on which no contributions are paid. This is a problem which must be resolved at the level of the FRY and RS governments."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Have you been following me, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see that there's a difference here between this translation and what you quoted at paragraph 118?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does the difference in translation change your conclusions in any way?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time if the first page of this document and page 45 and 46 of the English and 37 and 38 of the B/C/S be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This, again, is 65 ter 532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think Ms. Taseva prefers that I add these pages to the previous exhibit, if that is all right with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that would be preferable. May they be added to P312, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We can leave this exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, in normal times how are a country's expenses normally financed?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Normally a country is financed by taxes and that means taxation of its citizens, normal income tax. It would be taxes of businesses. It would be value-added tax and all other kinds of taxes. That would be the normal way of financing a country, at least in the long run. And of course you also have in the short run, you can also borrow money, but you can't rely on that forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, up until the middle of 1991, how were the entities of the former Yugoslavia financed?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: They were mostly financed by taxes, as any normal country or normal entity, to put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point in 1991, did this begin to change?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it did, and it was very dramatic. What happened in the second half of 1991 was that the SFRY, as such, started to be financed through the use of primary emissions --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Torkildsen, I'm going to cut you off for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter 6531. It's referred to in paragraph 18 of the report. We see this is a document called a "Proposal of Minimally Needed Funds that Need to be Provided in the Budget of the Federation for the Period July-September 1991." It's dated Belgrade, 21 July, 1991. Can we turn to page 3 in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, you cite to this document in paragraph 18 of your report. Can you describe what we see on the third page?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a proposal, then, on how to finance the SFRY budget in the period July to September 1991, and it is described here what kind of income they're relying on. As I previously stated, a normal country is financed by taxes, and as we can see here, customs and import tax is responsible for 37.3 per cent of the total financing of this budget. And if you see further down there, there's actually stated here "Original Income," 42.4 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: The term "original income" in this sense, and that's a term I've also seen in other documents, and that basically means the real income of a country, meaning its taxes. But what is interesting to note here is that the term used below what is mentioned as original income, it is stated "NBJ/Yugoslav People's Bank," and that is the same institution that I have labeled and also that we can see from other documents as the National Bank of Yugoslavia. And it's stated here that they will provide 52.3 per cent of the total income to this budget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt you a little bit, sir. In explaining what "original income" is, you said it's taxes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's basically taxes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that, in fact, we can quite safely say the 42.4 per cent of original taxes, together with the 37.3 per cent of customs and import taxes, that's the same source of income. It all comes from taxes. Therefore, taxes are contributing the sum of 42.4 and 37.3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost, Your Honour. For instance, it is also mentioned here, incomes and organs and organisations, and that would, for example, be the income from publicly-owned businesses and the profit from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But to a large extent, Your Honour, it's from taxes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but my problem is, if taxes contribute the sum of 37.3 and 42.4 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- from 100 per cent, there's very little for you left to have 52.3 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that, in fact, are you -- are we saying, then, that the total contribution is actually beyond -- the total income is not 100 per cent, it's 200 per cent, or whatever the figure is? And how does that work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It is actually also other types of income, like I pointed out. But most of the original income of a country would be from taxes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is it from -- from taxes for the current year, or is it money brought forward from the previous year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a proposal, so this is what they are planning for. They are planning to receive taxes in the order of 37.3 per cent. That is what they are assuming that they will get in taxes for this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. But then you also say, original income is also taxes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I am mindful -- I am mindful of the fact that there is a line drawn after other incomes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and if you say this is a completely different story from the one above the line, then I can follow you. But if it is still the same thing, that line means nothing and original income is defined as taxes, then I have the problem that I've just raised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can comment on that. The thing is that the original income which is stated here of 42.4 per cent, that is the sum of what is mentioned above. So if you add up all what is listed above there, you will reach the sum of 42.4 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That explains it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, you were mentioning you noted that 52.3 per cent of the income came from the Yugoslav People's Bank, funds.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe really what type of income that was or funds those were?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Is it possible to take this document to the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Please. And where do you want to focus, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: The last paragraph of that page where it is stated that: "The missing amount would be covered from the funds of the primary emission of the Yugoslav People's Bank and contributions by the SR and SAP."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, what does the term "primary emission" mean?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That means printing of money. What is stated here is that the deficit in the budget should be made off by the National Bank of Yugoslavia printing money in order to cover this budget deficit, cover the lack of original income.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, I'd seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: My mic is not working. That will be Exhibit P313, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the course of your review of documents, Mr. Torkildsen, beginning in 1992, did you become aware that the entities called the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina were established?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how were these new entities, if I can call them that, financed?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: They were very much financed by primary emissions provided to them by the National Bank of Yugoslavia in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so that the record is clear, sometimes in your report you use the phrase "primary issue." Are the two terms synonymous, "primary issue" and "primary emission"?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is the same. And also, sometimes in the budgets these are described as credits coming from the National Bank of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. But when they talk about credits, they're talking about these primary emissions, the printing of money.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina were financed very much by primary emissions from the National Bank of Yugoslavia, in 1992 the National Bank, just so that the record is clear, was part of -- was an institution of whom? What state?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: It was an institution of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter number 6531, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have just given 6531 an exhibit number, P313.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I misspoke. I was looking at the wrong number. Can we please see MFI 311. And can we go to page 12 in the B/C/S version, and there we see the appropriate page in the English version, and can we focus on the top half of the English version, please, or enlarge the top half a bit. It's a part of the "Official Gazette of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina" from the 8th of June, 1992, and it's a copy of a decision adopted on 14 May 1992 called "The Decision on the Use of Funds from Primary Issue."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, you refer to this document at paragraphs 16, 17, 62, and 73 of your report. What, if anything -- what do you take from this document that was significant for your work?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, the important article here is Article 1, where it is actually stated regarding the use of the funds. It is stated here that the funds that the RS has received from the National Bank of Yugoslavia, the "primary issues, shall be used in accordance with the decision of the National Bank of Yugoslavia ..." meaning that an entity of the FRY is deciding how the RS should use the money, the primary issue that they have received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would also like to, if I can please also comment on Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: It is stated in this article that in the end here, "with a negative balance to be settled once the National Bank of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is founded and starts operating." By this you can read that this is just a temporary arrangement that's going to be settled later on. But from other documents I have seen, this was not the case. But that will be explained from other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought this is MFI -- oh, you're now tendering the document. I'm sorry. Exhibit 311, marked for identification, is now being tendered for admission. It is admitted into evidence. It will be given an exhibit number, P311. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May we please leave this document and bring up 65 ter 6539.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, this is a document that you referred to at paragraphs 25 and 76 of your report. It's a decision from the 8th of July, 1992, by the Government of the Republika Srpska to take a loan from the National Bank of the Republika Srpska. Do you see that in the "Decision on Debiting of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the National Bank of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina"? Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you take that was significant from this document?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: The significance here being, as it's stated in Article 1 here, it is stated that due to the inadequate incoming assets that make up the original revenues, and then we are back to the previous proposal that I tried to explain. They are stating here that they do have inadequate resources regarding original income --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you here. When you use the pronoun "they," who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That means Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay, continue.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That they do not have the original income. They do not have the taxes to make up the revenue side of the budget. So instead they are taking up a loan from the National Bank, here of Republika Srpska, in order to finance their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at this point, then, by July, then the National Bank of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is functioning.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, whether it's functioning or not, that I can't state. But at least it has been established. It was established in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just make one more comment on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, do you want to wait for the comment, Mr. Lukic? Thank you. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it is mentioned here that this is actually a loan and that it shall be returned in ten equal annual installments, due on 15/12 each year, and that it should be repaid, then, in full by 15 December 1998, so it is basically a loan. But what happened in the Republika Srpska, the FRY and the RSK at -- during this time period was that it was hyperinflation, meaning that the nominal value of money at one point in time was not worth the same in two years -- two years later, meaning that if you took up a loan today and if you're going to repay it five years later, that means that you actually had to use no real money in order to pay it back because of the hyperinflation. You had hyperinflation at that time, particularly in 1993, of several thousand per cent during just one year, meaning that you repaid virtually nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There is also in the upper right-hand corner a note saying: "Payments to be adjusted with the needs of the army." Did you take anything of significance from that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Because most of the budgets of the RS was actually going to cover the needs of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would still seek to tender this. I believe my colleague has something to say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at this point in time, Your Honours, I challenge this and challenge the authenticity and the relevance of this document, both. And I'd like to state my arguments after the cross-examination of this witness, and could we have the MFI marking of this document now. But for your information, this is a document without a date, without a stamp, and without any signature, so may it just be marked for identification at this stage. The date column is empty and the second page of the original document is empty. With respect to the date, there's a place for the signature. But I'd like to leave those arguments for later, after I've conducted my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, as you respond, maybe you might also address the question of the handwritten markings on the B/C/S version which are absent, or maybe they are typed on the English side, and if you can sort of tell us what they mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: They are -- this was the passage that I referred to a few moments ago, Your Honour. Up at the top right-hand corner in handwriting it says: "Minister Subotic. Payments to be adjusted with the needs of the army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then we see a date there, and it's signed by Minister Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. That's the handwritten thing. Now, your colleague on the right side suggests that -- objects to the admission of this document at this point and said it could be MFIed. What's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe the document is relevant -- on its face, the document is relevant, Your Honours, because again it shows how now the Republika Srpska had to create its financing in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but that does not -- for relevance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour. Which is certainly relevant to Mr. Torkildsen's work. The handwritten note, Your Honour, at the top with the date, in the Prosecution's submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have explained that. Thank you so much. You have explained the handwritten note. Your learned friend talks of lack of date of the document, and I want to believe that you are saying that the date that we see on the document is the date of the handwritten remarks. But your friend says there's no date of the document, there's no signature there for -- he's challenging authenticity of the document, he will argue later. He suggests that the document be MFIed. What is your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the Trial Chamber's guidelines, the Trial Chamber tells us that the lack of a signature and the lack of a stamp or a seal does not by itself mandate the exclusion of a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend doesn't ask for exclusion. He says MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that, Your Honour. The Prosecution is willing to have it MFIed if that is the proper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 6539 is -- may it please be marked for identification and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P314, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Shall we take the first break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it is convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take the break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please see Prosecution 65 ter number 6526. Can we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, you cite to this document several times in your report, paragraphs 25, 35, 36, 39, 43 to 46, 50, 62, 73, and 87. It's actually a series of documents, but we'll stick with the first one. This is a report. It says: "National Bank of Yugoslavia, Strictly Confidential." And it reads that: "The management of the National Bank of Yugoslavia ..." this is the very first paragraph, " ... assigned Milivoj Miletic to analyse and review the operations of the National Bank of Republika Srpska in terms of the elements to implement the Monetary Policy Programme in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Republika Srpska, and the Republic of Serbian Krajina." And then in the next paragraph it explains that Mr. Miletic visited the National Bank of Republika Srpska between 4 and 8 April, 1994. And after analysing and reviewing the operations of the National Bank of Republika Srpska, he submits this report."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please, of the exhibit, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, there is a large paragraph in the middle of this page, beginning with the phrase "The first phase of the operations ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to direct you to this paragraph and more precisely to the middle of the paragraph, it's actually starting at the second full sentence: "This was a time when certain institutions of Republika Srpska were formed, including the National Bank. In such circumstances it was normal to issue primary money on the basis of previous experience, coming primarily from the National Bank of Yugoslavia." Is there anything that you take from this paragraph and what I've just read to you that you find significant for your report?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. This document corroborates what I have said and stated previously regarding that the National Bank of Yugoslavia was printing money in order to, as we have seen from the other documents, in order to finance budget deficits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understand it, this money was being printed by the Bank of Yugoslavia for the benefit of the Bank of Republika Srpska. It is being passed on to that bank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm trying to say is that at this point -- you said it was to finance budget deficits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, can I just -- since that is actually stated in the last part of this paragraph, where it is stated that -- just let me read that out. "About 14.3 per cent of these credits," the primary issues this means, "or 11.1 billion dinars were given through the banks, while the remaining 85.7 per cent or 67.7 billion dinars were given for the budget of Republika Srpska." So not all of the primary issues were given to the budget, but most of it was given to the budget. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there is another document that is part of 65 ter 6526. If we could please go to page 13 in the English version and page 11 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is an Official Note of a meeting between the governors of the National Bank of Yugoslavia, Republika Srpska, and Republika Srpska Krajina, held on the premises of the National Bank of Yugoslavia in Belgrade on 12 May 1994. And if you can direct your attention, Mr. Torkildsen, to about the middle of the page where it says: "It was concluded at the meeting that ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could then direct your attention to number 6.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "The National Bank of Republika Srpska and the National Bank of Republika Srpska Krajina operate as main branch offices of the National Bank of Yugoslavia and are solely dependent on its authority."

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then in the following subparagraph, 7: "It is the National Bank of Yugoslavia that has exclusive authority over the operating of the National Bank of Republika Srpska, the National Bank of Republika Srpska Krajina, and the commercial banks from Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina." Is there anything in subparagraph 6 and 7 that you found significant?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, actually, these two paragraphs speak for themselves. It states that the National Bank of Yugoslavia has got the control and directs the operations of the National Bank of Republika Srpska and the National Bank of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how do these two conclusions, if I may, fit or not with your report and your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: They fit perfectly. This is -- this describes in a short way what also the other documents point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender as a single exhibit pages 1 through 13 in the English version and page 1 through 12 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pages 1 to -- yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to stress once again, or rather I want to object to a portion of this document. The authenticity is what I'm objecting to. The first part of the document regarding Mr. Miletic's report, I'm not challenging authenticity there. But the second part of the document, which is the Official Note that we've just been talking about and heard testimony about, I'm challenging the authenticity of that for a number of reasons, one of which is the document has no signature or stamp. But what is more troubling, as far as I'm concerned and that leads me to doubt the authenticity of this document is the following: The fact that it is part of this report and attached to Mr. Miletic's report and the date of the official report is after the report itself. It's a later date. So you can see that the Official Note about that particular meeting was compiled on the 12th of May, 1994, whereas Mr. Miletic's report is dated -- well, the date is after the control, from the period from the 6th to the 8th of April, 1994. And I have to stress another point that is also troubling with respect to this Official Note. It's another document, a 65 ter Prosecution document, which -- this is 65 ter 6557, is the document number. I don't know if Mr. Saxon wants to tender that document, too. But anyway, it has the identical contents. Looking at the contents of that document, of this Official Note, it's the same but written in quite a different form, using different language. And I'm sure you know that there was the Ljkavian and Ekavinan dialects on the territory of the former Yugoslavia that were used. And the document is likewise not signed. If possible, at this stage, I'd like this to be given an MFI number so that I can cross-examine the witness and you can determine the authenticity of this document. But I have no objections to be made with respect to Mr. Miletic's report being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before I ask Mr. Saxon to respond, if you can just clear a sentence that you mention here at page 37, lines -- starting from line 15. You say: "So you can see that the Official Note of that particular meeting was compiled on the 12th of May, 1994, whereas Mr. Miletic's report is dated -- well, the date is after the control, from the period of the 6th to the 8th of April, 1994." I'm not quite sure by what is meant "after the control," if that is what you said, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This 65 ter document has 40 pages, Your Honour, the entire document. First of all, we have the report on that control by Mr. Miletic. That's the first part of the document. And then we have six attachments, supplements. And it's a 65 ter document. One of those supplements is this Official Note, and the date at which the meeting that the Official Note refers to is later than the report itself, which leads me to doubt the authenticity of the document and raises a number of questions in my mind, because logically if you are providing a report, then you're providing supplementary documents following the period before the report, before it's written, not the subsequent period and after the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is not submitting that -- if I can step back for a moment. Pages 1 through 13 of the English -- excuse me, I believe 1 through -- the first document in 65 ter 6526 is the report of Mr. Miletic about the work that he did in April of 1994. 65 ter 6526 contains a series of documents, Your Honour, and it is not the Prosecution's position that the following documents were part of Mr. Miletic's report. Certainly there's no connection -- the documents do not speak to each other. The Official Note of the meeting between the governors of the National Banks, which is the document which Mr. Lukic would like to have MFIed, it's describing a separate event. Mr. Miletic is describing the work that he did and the analysis that he made. This Official Note is simply a different event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if you and your learned friend can be brought onto the same wavelength. Are you saying the note is not an attachment attached by Mr. Miletic? It's an attachment attached by the Prosecution, just collecting unrelated documents and putting them together perhaps because they are talking about the same subject, maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was put together this way because this is how the Prosecution received this particular -- this particular series of documents. It received them together so we kept them together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question slightly differently worded. Is the note -- does the note not form part of attachments of the report by Mr. Miletic after his investigations? Because I suspect this is the position that Mr. Lukic is taking, and I understand you to be saying these documents are unrelated. Therefore, if they are unrelated, it doesn't form part of Mr. Miletic's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour. I'm simply saying that the Prosecution simply does not know whether Mr. Miletic attached the Official Note to his report or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I simply -- to be honest, I simply can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But the Prosecution is seeking to tender Mr. Miletic's report with the note as an attachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So you are not tendering the note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This 65 ter number is 40 pages long, and obviously I don't want to give the Chamber 40 additional pages to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was these two pieces that the Prosecution felt were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine, fine, fine. Do the 40 pages of the document you want to tender, include the note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic's objection is that tendering them in that form, he is given the impression that all those documents are part and parcel of the report by Mr. Miletic, and he says he finds this strange because the report was drafted around April and now an attachment to this report is dated May, 12th of May, long after the report has been drawn. This is the basis on which he is objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And unless you are able to say to us that the note is not part of Mr. Miletic's report, then Mr. Lukic's objection has substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I take your point, and I am not able -- I am not able to say that the note is not part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. He is then saying -- he suggests that we MFI rather than admit at this stage, until this problem is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No objection at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 65 ter 6526, pages 1 to 13 in the English and I think 1 to 12 in the B/C/S are marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm very sorry, Your Honour. My learned colleague did not object to the admission of Mr. Miletic's report. That is what he told us. His only objection is to the admission of the Official Note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies to you. Pages 1 to 13 of the 65 ter 6526, together with the note, I don't know how -- what is your 65 ter number of the note? It is part of that whole thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you are now back-pedaling. You want an admission to MFI the entire 40 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to be MFIed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The report of Mr. Miletic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. In its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- which is the first ten pages in English and the first nine pages in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what you're tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not the note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I have dealt with these documents in detail and I've followed your arguments, and I know the answer to this question, at least from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but you see, at this point we're dealing with an objection that is raised by the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And unfortunately it keeps you out of the loop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If there's anything, your lawyer should have taken instructions on how those documents relate to one another. And if he hasn't, the only solution is to mark them for identification, and once you have given him proper instructions, he can come and give us an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's okay. I just want to be clear what it is you are tendering at this stage. You are tendering 65 ter 526, pages 1 to 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the same 65 ter number, pages 1 to 9 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. That's all?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That 65 ter 6526, pages 1 to 10 in English and 1 to 9 in B/C/S are marked for identification. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those pages will be Exhibit P315, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter number 6528. Your Honour, I'm not trying to aggravate you or your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not aggravated at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. It's simply this: Your order -- what you did in your order was you marked for identification the pages from 6526 which Mr. Lukic does not object to their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I see that now. Thank you so much. I see the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can I perhaps simplify your work and Ms. Taseva's work. This same Official Note that is the basis of the objection, as Mr. Lukic pointed out, has a separate 65 ter number, because we've actually received these documents from different sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just the note by itself is 65 ter 6557. Perhaps for your organisational purposes, it would be simpler simply to mark for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That explains the objection. That answers Mr. Lukic's problem. Because he referred to 65 ter 6557 in his objection and said now there are two documents exactly the same. So it is exactly the same document, sir. This note does not form part of Mr. Miletic's report, from that explanation. It comes completely independently. It is just the convenience of the Prosecution that they put them together, as I understand you now. Okay. While you do that, on the point that you have raised with the Bench, may Exhibit P315 please be admitted into evidence and not marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Exhibit P315, marked for identification, will now get exhibit status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's where you thought you were giving us grief, and we were giving you grief. It was my fault. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's no problem, Your Honour. I will move on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter 6528. It's there. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, you refer to this document at page 73 of your report, and we see this is a "Decision on the Adoption of the Rebalance of Republika Srpska Budget for 1993." Up at the top we see it was dated 25 March 1994. And I'd like to take you first to Article 1. What does Article 1 tell us?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: It actually states the total amount in the -- what has been translated here as the budget of Republika Srpska, but I would like to draw your attention to the -- to the data which is listed as 25 March 1994, talking here about the budget for 1993. So the way that I read this, this is closer to being the final annual accounts of the Republika Srpska for 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's how we should understand the word "rebalancing"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's at least how I interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. If you look at Article 2, we see the same total figure, the last line, and we see a figure for original income, and then we see a much larger figure for credits. Can you explain what, if anything, is significant, please.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: The significance being here that, as explained earlier, original income, which is mainly made up of taxes, accounts for almost nothing of the total budget, while the credits, here meaning the primary emission, accounts for almost the whole of the income side of this budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page in English, please, and perhaps scroll down in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we look at the -- if we look at this list of amounts of money, again, at the very bottom under "Total Expenses," we see the same total. Is there anything in this list that you found significant?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, as you pointed out, you see the total expenses there. I'm just looking for the figure here that specifically shows what is going for the army, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we scroll up a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see it in the B/C/S version, but I can't see it in the translation here, because the B/C/S version shows the figure, starting off 700 and something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's still the wrong page of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. Can we go to the third page, please, in English, and the following page in B/C/S. I apologise. Can we move back one page in the English version, please, and if we can focus on the very bottom of that list, we see Article 1, the full total, 732 billion dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the list on page 2, do you see an item called "Current Expenses of the Army"?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's exactly the point. It shows that the expenses of the army is close to taking up more or less the whole budget, and I calculated that amount of 700 and something to account for 95 -- 95.6 per cent of the total budget is actually used for the expenses of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Document 65 ter 6528 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, at paragraphs 51 through 60 of your report, and that's pages 19 through 21 of the English and pages 18 to 21 of the B/C/S, you discuss something known as the Public Accounting Office, or the SDK. What was this institution, and what did it do?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That was the institution responsible for making the transfers of money between -- well, both within the FRY and also including the RS and the RSK, meaning that this institution and -- basically, the SDK, that's an institution making sure that the mechanism is working for transferring money. It's also been translated as the Public Accounting Service, the State Accounting Service, and other various translations. So that's basically the two that the -- that the FRY and the RS and the RSK is using to transfer money between them. Just to make a moment of that as well, this is not a new invention.
