This was something that also existed back in the days of the SFRY, but then of course it also included the other republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where is it located, headquartered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you aware whether there were, for lack of a better term, branch offices of the SDK in different areas?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. There were offices all over the -- both the FRY, the RS, and the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving on, can we please see Prosecution P00149, please, and if we could go to page 127 in the English and page 111 in the B/C/S. And the English -- the English translation has doc ID 0060-7339.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This document, the entire document, is an analysis of the combat readiness of the VRS. It's dated April 1993. And the full title is "Analysis of the Combat Readiness and Activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992." Mr. Torkildsen, if we can focus on page 127, please, of the English. First of all, you'll see there's a subheading: "Planning of the Development and Financing of the VRS Army." That's at the top of the page. We'll see in bullet points there are three different stages that are discussed with three different time periods. And then in the next full paragraph, there is a line beginning with "The Order of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence." Of what government, country, or institution did the Federal Secretariat for National Defence belong to?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: The FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can focus on the next paragraph, beginning with "In the second stage ..." please, if we can zoom in on that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That paragraph begins: "In the second stage, the Ministry of Defence, i.e., the Government of Republika Srpska, took over the entire financing burden, except for the personal expenditures (salaries and benefits) of officers, non-commissioned officers, soldiers working under contract, and workers who remained in or joined the Army of Republika Srpska from the former JNA." Did you take anything that was significant from this paragraph, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, because the soldiers and also these other personnel categories that are being mentioned here, they were financed through the budget of Republika Srpska and that's -- that's the significance. And if I also may add, this is part of a military document, and as I stated in the beginning, this was a typical military document also containing financial information, and that is why I reviewed it. And what comes out later in this document, you will see how the money was actually spent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In this paragraph there's a phrase beginning with "Except for ..." Do you see that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So there are some categories of persons which would not fall under the financing of the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then who would be financing those categories - officers, non-commissioned officers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: They would be financed from the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 128 in the English, and it would be 112 in the B/C/S, I hope. And can we focus on the very bottom of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see a subheading, 7.1, "The Spending of the Army Budget," where we see at its sessions in July 1992 the Assembly of what was then the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina approved funds for financing the army in the July through December 1992 period. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then it gives the amount, more than 53 billion dinars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Trillion, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't mean to argue with you, Mr. President. I thought it was in the billions, but I will defer to you. It even says in the English translation, written out, "53 billion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you're right. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can we turn to the next page in the English, please, 129, and can we focus in on the paragraph near the top, beginning with "It is important ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, that paragraph tells us, or the analysis tells us that: "It is important to mention that the salaries of officers, non-commissioned officers, soldiers under contract and workers in the RS Army, who until 19 May 1992 had been members of the JNA, continued to be the responsibility of the FR Yugoslavia, so that these expenditures were not debited from the budget of the Army of Republika Srpska." Why, if at all, was this significant for you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: This paragraph clearly states out that the officers and also some other personnel categories continued to be the responsibility of the FRY Yugoslavia, meaning that they continued to be on that payroll and was financed from the FRY directly, in contrast to the ordinary soldiers who were financed by the budget of Republika Srpska that again received the money from the National Bank of Yugoslavia. So this is a direct financing, while the financing of the budget or through the budget is actually an indirect financing. But the source of the money all originates from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we now focus our attention on the table at the bottom of this page, please. In the English version it's at the bottom. I don't -- yeah, we need to move to the next page in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This table, Mr. Torkildsen, says that it "shows the amounts spent by individual support elements." And the first purpose, if we see in the far left-hand column, says "Personnel Outlays." Was this significant for you, that particular item?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I think it's interesting here to note that actually the salaries of conscripts and ordinary soldiers accounts for as much as close to 60 per cent of the total budget for the army here, and as I noted from another part of this document, is that the reasoning for this is that the ordinary soldiers, on average, in the RS Army in 2002 has got an average strength of 212.000 soldiers. So that probably explains the huge percentage going to the ordinary soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can leave this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And again, if we can -- just to tie this together. The money that would have been allocated by the FRY to the Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- for the needs of the Army of the Republika Srpska, where would that money originate from?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That would originate from the National Bank of Yugoslavia in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how was that money financed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: By -- well, it was basically by primary emissions, printing money.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. How long did this financing of the VRS through the issue -- through the use of primary emissions go on?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That went on until early 1994, most likely January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, this may get a bit complicated, but what happened at that time is that a new governor was put in place in the National Bank of Yugoslavia in Belgrade, Mr. Avramovic, and the National Bank of Yugoslavia at that time pegged the dinar to the Deutschemark, meaning that it was set at parity, again meaning that 1 Deutschemark was the equivalent of 1 dinar, the purpose of this being to stop the enormous inflation. And what they did at that time was that they stopped -- and I mean "them," the National Bank of Yugoslavia stopped using primary emission as a tool to covering the budget deficits. That was both the budget deficits of the FRY as such and also the budget deficits of the RS and the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how was the deficit financed at this stage now, or was it because now the stronger dinar was able to reduce the deficit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a very good question, and I don't have a complete answer to that, because I've not been able to locate, for instance, the RS budgets for -- or annual accounts for 1994 or 1995. But I've seen a similar thing from the RSK budget for 1994, and that actually shows that they got more money in from taxation and other sources, meaning original income, than they had previously. But I've also seen from other documents that the FRY, meaning the National Bank of Yugoslavia, was still providing cash to both the RS and the RSK, but the difference now was that the National Bank of Yugoslavia had asked the RS and the RSK national banks to back up these demands with hard currency. So they actually had to deposit hard currency, here I would assume mostly meaning Deutschemarks, in order to receive new fresh dinars. So it was no longer a gift by the FRY to cover the budgets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can step back from this topic for a moment, Mr. Torkildsen. When we were looking at the last document, and we saw that there was financing from the FRY for certain members of the Army of Republika Srpska, do you know from which institution or institutions that money would have come from?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That would have come from the 30th Personnel Centre with the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned, in answer to Judge Moloto's question, that the money provided from the FRY to the RSK or the Republika Srpska, after this change in 1994, was no longer a gift by the FRY to cover the budget. Having said that, did the FRY continue to provide some kinds of financial assistance to the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did, in terms of -- I've seen several documents showing that both the VRS and the RSK army requesting cash from the National Bank of Yugoslavia. But mainly the big difference there for me in analysing this is that from the period 1994 and onwards, there is a lack of documentation compared to the previous period in order for me to conclude how this was done. I can see that the VRS and the institutions of the RS are requesting money, but I can't really see how this is done in practice. So I just have to rely on a previous document stating that they were actually planning at least for the institutions of the RS to actually deposit foreign currency in order to receive new dinars. That's all I can conclude. What actually happened, I do not know for sure after January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to 65 ter 645.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do so, what do we do with P00149?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That can be removed now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not wanting to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This number that you gave when you put it on the screen, you said it was P00149.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In short, are you saying this is Exhibit P149 in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and it's my understanding that the entire document has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. I wasn't aware of that. Okay, you can call the -- what do you want now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next document would be 65 ter 645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a document entitled "Aide Memoire for the Coordination of Tasks at the VJ/Yugoslav Army/GS/General Staff on 17 December 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please. The document is dated December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On this particular page we can see it's sent from the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army to the Office of the Chief of the General Staff, and it refers to the coordination of tasks between the VJ and the SVK that will be attended by persons from the Main Staff of the SVK, and then there are proposals below for matters of discussion. If we scroll down to the bottom, we see that it's signed and stamped by the Chief of the Office of the SVK Commander, Colonel Cedo Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page. Actually, it would be page 13 in the English, and I am embarrassed because I'm not sure that I have the B/C/S, but I might. It's page 10 in the B/C/S version. And if we can focus on the last paragraph, please, the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see a subparagraph (c), "New Requests." And then we are told: "We have learned unofficially that of the above total balance of requirements for 1994, the Federal Government will only be able to provide USD 850 million for all three armed forces instead of USD 3.29 billion, i.e., 25.82 per cent of the stated requirements. For the SVK, this would amount to USD 79.43 million instead of USD 307.30 million." Did you take anything from this paragraph, Mr. Torkildsen, that was relevant or significant for your report?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. As we can see here, it is the FRY government who's actually planning to fund all three armies in -- also in 1994, but they are getting less than they originally had planned for. As I mentioned previously, even if the financing through primary emissions stopped, at least they were still planning to continue the financing in 1994, by then a different method. But then again, as I pointed out, when it comes to 1994, there has been a lack of documents for me to review. It's also notable here to see that at this point in time they are talking about their requirements in US dollars and not in dinars anymore, and that is, of course, because of the hyperinflation. These dinar denominations didn't mean anything anymore because the value changed from one day to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please pull up 65 ter number 6548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we help, Mr. Perisic? Are you okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, everything is okay. The accused has his headsets on so he might have been a little loud in communicating with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can enlarge the English. Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 5th of May, 1994, to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command. We see it's signed -- or the accuracy of the transcription is certified by Commander Dzoko Trifkovic. We also see the name of Commander Major General Stanislav Galic to the left. And the document, if you see -- well, at the top, the subject is "Conscript Salaries for the Month of February," and it's an announcement. In the first paragraph it describes how the authors have received a letter, referring to a document from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, dated the 4th of May, 1994, the previous day of this document. And if you look at subparagraph 3, Mr. Torkildsen, it says: "In our daily contacts with the National Bank of Yugoslavia, due to enormous problems we have so far been unable to secure that cash. They have promised us that they will secure the cash by 6 May 1994, so that payment would commence on 9 May 1994 at the latest." And you cited this document at paragraph 119 of your report. What did you take from this document that was significant?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: The document shows that one corps or unit within the VRS is still requesting cash from the National Bank of Yugoslavia, and they point that they have a problem receiving that cash and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could now see 65 ter number 6521, please, which is a document referred to at paragraph 98 of Mr. Torkildsen's report. The document is called "Official Note from the Talks Between Representatives of the RSK Government and President Slobodan Milosevic." It's directed to the Ministry of the Republic of Serbia. Can we see more of the bottom of the page, please. The first paragraph talks about a meeting held on the 12th of November, 1992, hosted by the president of the Republic of Serbia, where there were representatives of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Government of the Republic of Serbia. President Slobodan Milosevic, we see, was there, prime Minister Radovan Bozovic, and also we see the President of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Goran Hadzic. And following the first paragraph, we see a sentence, or part of a sentence, saying: "At the meeting the mode of financial assistance to the Krajina until the end of the year was agreed." And the following large paragraph -- well, the following paragraph discusses defence, and an outline creating the RSK's army and its financing was brought up. And then we see in the following paragraph: "The President, Mr. Milosevic, agreed to the concept of creating a defence system of the Krajina which would be based on about 23.000 people in the police ..." And later on in that paragraph -- actually, if we go to the next paragraph, we see that: "President Milosevic said that funds for maintaining equipment should be planned via the Army of Yugoslavia and that he would help in the implementation of this and that the Army of Yugoslavia should finance the active officers and civilians who stayed behind in the Krajina." Did you find anything significant about this passage?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It is stated here that the funds for maintaining the equipment should be planned via the Army of Yugoslavia and that they should invest in that direction, and further on, that the Army of Yugoslavia, meaning here the VJ, should finance the active officers, meaning the army officers in the RSK army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we scroll further to the bottom of the English, perhaps it's on the next page of the English, we see that the document is from President of the Republic, Goran Hadzic. It was received on the 24th of June, 1993. Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just misspoke because I was looking at a different document. The document that was just admitted was from the Minister of defence, Stojan Spanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter 6116, a document which Mr. Torkildsen refers to at paragraph 102 of his report. And we see this is a document from the Republika Srpska Krajina, Cabinet of the President. It's sent from the President of the Republic, Goran Hadzic. At the bottom we see it was processed -- it was received on the 24th of June, 1993. And if we could focus, please, first on the paragraph that begins with the line "We need help ..." It's the third full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In that paragraph, it says that: "We need help in technical maintenance of weapons and acquisition of ammunition, grease, and petrol. All weapons and ammunition we get from the Yugoslav Army." And then the last sentence, it says: "We are not financially in position to make up for medium and general service which may be done by the institutions of the Yugoslav Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could then focus, please, on the paragraph lower down that begins with the word "Representatives ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says that: "Representatives of the SAK Headquarters together with their commandant presented these problems at the last meeting with the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army on 24 May 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we be reminded? What does "SAK" stand for?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not familiar with the acronym SAK. Excuse me, Serbian Army of Krajina. It's at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, it's an English acronym.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then there is a paragraph that says -- it's a request, actually. "We ask you to try to exercise your authority and influence the realisation of our requests presented to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army as soon as possible." Mr. Torkildsen, what, if anything, did you find significant in this document?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: This document corroborates all the documents that I have seen that the RSK army didn't have their own financial resources, so they had to request that from -- from the FRY. And here they are specifically asking the then-President, Mr. Milosevic to use his influence over the VJ army in order to get that financial assistance that they need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would seek to tender this document, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon, would you like an early one? You don't sound very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour, and I do see the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just saying, in light of your condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour -- no, normally we would break at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, it's probably -- it probably makes sense before I go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please see Prosecution 65 ter 6556.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a request for a cash grant from the National Bank of Republic of Serbian Krajina, dated 24 July 1995, and the request is addressed to the National Bank of Yugoslavia, the Treasury Directorate, General Director Vojo Tomic. Mr. Torkildsen --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we scroll down towards the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, the first paragraph says: "Please authorise a new grant of cash, totaling 10 million dinars for the requirements of the National Bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." And the next paragraph: "Since we are nearing the end of July, and the deadline for paying the army, police, pensions, et cetera, is approaching, our needs are great." And it says: "In order for the National Bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to provide the funds necessary to cover the requirements cited, it needs a further 10 million dinars in addition to the cash in its own treasury." You cite to this request at paragraph 72 of your report. What did you find significant about this document?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I think the most significant is that as late as in July 1995, the RSK National Bank is still requesting cash from the National Bank of Yugoslavia, and it also states what the use of the money will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we please see Prosecution 65 ter 6523.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a document addressed to the investigating judge of the district court in Belgrade, and it's an appeal by the defendant Slobodan Milosevic against the ruling to detain him. At the very bottom -- at the end of the third page in English, Mr. Milosevic -- we see Mr. Milosevic has signed it, and the date of this document is 2 April 2001. Mr. Torkildsen --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Taseva. Can we go back to the first page, please. Actually, I misspoke. Ms. Taseva was correct. Can we go back to the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Torkildsen, the second paragraph of the second page begins with the word "As regards ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic writes: "As regards the resources spent for weapons, ammunition, and other needs of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, these expenditures constituted a state secret and because of state interests could not be indicated in the Law on the Budget, which is a public document." And further down that paragraph, in the middle of the paragraph four lines from the bottom, we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we scroll up in the English, please. We're on the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see Mr. Milosevic says -- this is five lines from the bottom: "... and this was not made public ..." he's talking about expenditures, "... because it was a state secret, as was everything else that was provided for the Army of Republika Srpska." Mr. Torkildsen, what did you take from that document that is significant for your report?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: This statement signed by Mr. Milosevic corroborates exactly with some of the other documents that I've been through this morning in terms of pointing out the assistance that they gave to the Army of Republika Srpska being a state secret and not clearly apparent from the budgets. Because when we look at, for instance, the budget of the RS, there is no mentioning there of the primary emissions coming from Belgrade. In order to actually establish that, we have to look at all the other documents and how they relate to each other and put it into a context, and then we can see the pattern of how this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying in the state documents there was no mention of primary emissions in the funding of the RS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No, I'm sorry, Your Honour. It was clearly a mentioning of the primary issues, but there was no mentioning in the RS budget that this originated from Belgrade. Like, for instance, the Miletic report that we looked at - that was the confidential and not the public document, in the public domain - that explains that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the record, this is referred to at paragraphs 15 and 99 of Mr. Torkildsen's report. Your Honour, I would seek to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, at paragraphs 5 to 15 of your report, you provide your conclusions. Could you briefly describe the conclusions that you reached based on the work that you performed.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. My conclusion is that from the year -- from the end of 1991 and until early 1994, the main financing source of the RS was the primary emissions that they received from the National Bank of Yugoslavia. And I would also like to add that after that point in time I have not seen any other sources of finance for either the RS or the RSK. Throughout the whole period the main source of finance for these entities there, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and also the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, you said "throughout the whole period."

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you give us the years that you're referring to now?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period 1991 and including 1994, and also at least certain periods of 1995 where they were still requesting cash, as pointed out in the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, can we call up 65 ter 6557, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. While we're waiting for this 65 ter 557, Mr. Torkildsen, would you make the caveat to that conclusion that you are reaching that as late as 1995 there was still yet a requisition from the RSK for that 10 billion dinar to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So beyond 1994 there was at least that 10 billion request.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they were still requesting cash. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you don't know whether that request was met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't seen any evidence to that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, not to beat a dead horse, the document in front of you is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- is an Official Note. It is a slightly different version of the Official Note that we discussed earlier today that was part of 65 ter 6526. I've discussed this with my colleague, Mr. Lukic, and what I propose to do simply now is if this Official Note, 6557, could be marked for identification at this time, and then Mr. Lukic, I believe, will make his arguments about the admission of this document after cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if you can clear me, you're saying something slightly different from what you said earlier. Earlier when we discussed Mr. Miletic's report, you indicated that that attachment there, that Official Note in that report, is exactly the same as this one, or at least Mr. Lukic said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I was wrong, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you were wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there are two separate documents, slightly different?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Exhibit 6557 -- I beg your pardon. 65 ter 6557 is admitted -- is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P323, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Torkildsen. Let me introduce myself. My name is Novak Lukic. I'm an attorney from Belgrade, and on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Perisic, I'm going to ask you a few questions now. First of all, some introductory clarifications is what I'd like to seek from you. Now, this report, the report that we're discussing today, you compiled, first and foremost, for the requirements of the Prosecution in the Slobodan Milosevic trial; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in that same trial you appeared in court and testified with respect to your expert report and answered questions during the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Milosevic himself; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This report of yours, with certain additions and amendments, in fact, represented, if I can put it this way, the substance of your expert finding before the International Court of Justice, pursuant to the complaint made by Bosnia-Herzegovina and the lawsuit against the state community of Serbia and Montenegro, which was conducted two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also, as far as I was able to see, for the needs and requirements of the OTP, you compiled another report, expert report, in the Milosevic trial which was called a supplemental report, or something like that, and was linked to your analysis of the financing of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and the Army of Yugoslavia by or, rather, through, via, if I can put it that way the companies that were established in Cyprus. That was what you focused on in your expert report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that expert report was not admitted either in the Milosevic trial or in the Milutinovic trial. It was tendered, but it was not admitted as an exhibit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I can only answer to the Milosevic trial. That's correct, it was not admitted. The Milutinovic trial, I do not know anything about so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you a few questions about your CV so that we can clarify our discussion this morning and your morning testimony, and for that I'm going to use what I have in front of me, which is Exhibit P309, but I might be referring to your first expert report, the initial one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could have that brought up. It is 65 ter -- just a moment. Let me check the number. 6527 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, here it goes. You'll remember this first report, or, rather, CV that you attached to your 2002 expert report, your curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for clarity's sake, Mr. Lukic, what we have on the screen now is what you call 6527. What happened to P309, which you were calling -- which you also called?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I might refer to -- I think I'm going to focus on this particular CV for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You studied at the University of Manchester, and you studied in the field of management; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I looked through the programme of that particular university, and I'm interested in knowing what it was at the time, and I did not see that there were any studies, any course, which would cover public finances and macro-economic policy. Now, at the time that you were there, was there any course or subject taught from that particular area?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Actually, finance was a big part of this. There were both courses in both macro-economics and micro-economics. Just to clarify, because I think there have been some big changes with that University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology after I left. I now think that a part of UMIST has merged with Manchester University, the main university in Manchester, so I think it would be rather difficult to look back to what was actually taught. But that's an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what do we understand in the context of your discussion to be macro-economics and micro-economics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Macro-economics is exactly the issues we're dealing with today regarding how, for instance, a country overall is being financed, instead of the micro-economics of how it -- actually businesses go about conducting their finances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any final paper to write? And if so, what was the subject of that thesis or paper?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Are you thinking about my master's degree or my bachelor's degree?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm still at your studies in Manchester, but I'll ask you about your post-graduate studies in due course. In Manchester, did you have any final paper to write?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you attended post-graduate studies for one year in London, I believe, and it says that this was in shipping, trade, and finance. That's what it says in your CV.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any final paper to write there? And if so, what was the subject?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a final paper, and my final paper was "The Attractiveness of Shipping Shares to the Institutional Investors on the Oslo Stock Exchange."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I don't think I could repeat that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can read it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in your post-graduate studies, within the frameworks of the course you just mentioned, was there any specialisation course with topics such as monetary unions, public finances, or inflationary trends, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, I did a lot of -- well, it was focusing on -- the whole study was focusing on financing, but it was not very much at the macro level, mostly at the micro level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, I understand your CV in the global sense as saying that professionally you focused on research work; that during your career you were a researcher and investigator. So let me ask you: Did you ever write a professional paper, and were those papers printed? I don't see that in your CV, either in the first CV you provided or in this latest CV either.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I've never written any professional papers regarding macro-financing, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, in actual fact, would I be right in saying that your professional work, first and foremost, was that for 13 years you dealt with research and investigation and establishing some omissions or faults in companies, but you dealt primarily with police research work, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: To a certain extent, you are right. But as a financial investigator, a lot of the work that I carried out was analysis and evaluating documents and trying to identify how they -- how the facts related to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the focus of your activity was largely -- well, I'd like to focus on the period until 2002 principally. They were fraud, corruption, bribery, in various institutions for which you -- which you were in charge of investigating and monitoring. Would that be generally right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: It would be very much a matter of following the money trail. In order to solve a financial crime, you would have to follow the money from where it starts and to whose pockets it ends up in, which is very much the same as in this case. It's just that in this case it's a much broader scale, but the principles being the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before you became an investigator for the OTP, in your investigations you did not look into public finances, did you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, I did look into public financing in cases -- actually, regards -- regarding defrauding the state. Unfortunately, there are a lot of cases out there that involves people basically stealing public money.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we take a look at page 2 of this document that we've just had on our screens. It says there -- well, I'm sorry, but we have to go back to page 1, the bottom part of page 1, and I'm interested in the period between 1994 up to 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm reading the B/C/S version, so it's a bit -- it says you were special investigator for Norway of the Norwegian National Authority for Investigation and Prosecution of Economic and Environmental Crime. So that's the period before you became an investigator in the Hague Tribunal, or rather the OTP of the Tribunal. So for a series of years, you worked for that Norwegian agency, and it has an acronym, I believe, OKOKRIM, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I took a look at that. Would you agree with me when I say that the report of the organisation called "Group of States Against Corruption," that in 2002 they ascertained that Norway had the least number of cases of corruption and embezzlement, and so on. Do you agree with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: It depends compared to, actually, which other countries?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't mean to interrupt the response. I can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Finish off your answer, Mr. Torkildsen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, Norway, unfortunately, is ranked as the most corrupt country in the Nordic region, but it's very low on the international scale. But we do have, unfortunately, quite a number of corruption cases. Had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No longer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we still have some ongoing cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be possible for the Prosecution to receive a copy of the report that Mr. Lukic mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it with me, but certainly I will provide it to the Prosecution. I hadn't prepared to tender that into evidence. I just wanted to check out my information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We would love to have it handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's something else that I read in that particular report, and it's this: That from 1997 to 2000, this organisation, OKOKRIM, that you worked for, launched two investigations for corruption, and that during that period of time nobody was convicted of that crime. That's what I read, so would that be right? Do you agree with that? Do you know anything more about that? Because it was during the period that you worked there, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: What I remember from that period, I investigated one case that I actually spent more than three years on. It was a big corruption case involving a Norwegian National being employed by UNICEF. As I mentioned this morning, it involved investigations in approximately 15 to 16 countries throughout Europe, including the US. So that was basically what kept me busy at that time. And the person in question, he was found guilty, and that must have been in 2001, because I remember I had to leave the Tribunal in order to go to Oslo to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that period while you were working in that Norwegian agency, I assume that you worked in teams. Did you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I also assume that the teams included professionals from different professions, for example, economics; another example, law; then various other specialties; forensic experts, and so on. I assume that that's how your teamwork functioned.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, in those teams of yours, were there public prosecutors included and were you subordinate to the rules governing the public prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Each of the teams was led by a senior public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I also assume that it was the public prosecutor that set the guidelines for you, that is to say, to steer you in one direction or another and provide perhaps legal advice linked to what the prosecutor was interested in for him to be able to take action should the need arise.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That would be his job, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you also have to be informed about legal regulations during that period of time that were in force and were important for your cases. For example, if you were there supposed to establish whether a person in a company was responsible for something and if they did hold a responsible position in a company, you would have to know what their legal responsibilities were.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you were investigating a case, corruption in a company, for example, you had to know what laws applied to the functioning of that company to see whether there were any irregularities or omissions in the work of such a company.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that could be relevant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you a few questions linked to your work and your methodology, and you told us something about that to a certain extent in your introduction here today. Paragraph 1, in particular, do you have your report in front of you? I'd like you to be provided with a copy if you haven't got it, because I'd like to refer to paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Torkildsen be provided with a hard copy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to bring it up on the screen, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Yes, we can do that too, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, what would you like to do that with 6527?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender that document into evidence as well, and I apologise for not doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D9, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we put up paragraph 1, ERN number -- let me just check that. It is Mr. Torkildsen's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is P310, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 1, please. We'll just wait to have it up in English. Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Anyway, this is what you say. You say that: "The Office of the Prosecutor asked me to identify, review, analyse and write a report on a large number of documents obtained from the OTP." And then you go on to say that the scope of your report was "to determine what, if any, during the period of 1991 to 1995, financial support was provided by organisations under the alleged de jure and de facto control of Slobodan Milosevic ..." and then it goes on to mention the areas that were called Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska. That's a summary of paragraph 1. Mr. Torkildsen, can you tell us how you, as an economist, understand the concept of de jure and de facto. You must have had a position on that concept given your assignment.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: The de jure control would be actually the control you have in fact of your official position, but it doesn't exactly mean that you can also influence on the control of other people, even if, according to your official position, that is not the case. So there is a big difference there. So it can be in terms of your personality, who you are connected to, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that would be de facto control, what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Somebody that doesn't have direct -- well, that's where you make the distinction. Yes, I understand right. Now, the person from the OTP who gave you this assignment and stipulated it as set out in paragraph 1, did the Prosecutor who gave you the assignment tell you what they, that is to say, the OTP, considers were organisations under de jure control of Mr. Milosevic and what were the de facto ones? Did they present their views in the matter?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, as it is stated here, "the alleged control," and then that, again, means what was alleged by the Prosecution. Again, that means the indictment of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For you to know who, according to the Prosecution, were the organs under the de jure control of Slobodan Milosevic, you had to be aware of the regulations giving that person his de jure remit, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, I -- presumably at that time I did have some knowledge about the regulations. It's okay that I only -- well, that I dealt mainly with the financial documents, but of course I also read other documents that were provided to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also thought, Mr. Lukic, that the witness said that the allegations of de jure and de facto were as made in the indictment by the Prosecution. It was not a determination by him, but a determination by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood that, Your Honour, but I wanted to ask the question nonetheless because I wanted to link that up to his conclusions in paragraph 124, in order to be able to see how he was able to establish and ascertain Milosevic's de jure and de facto relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Torkildsen -- well, anyway, in the Milosevic trial, you testified and said that you hadn't read the constitution when asked by Mr. Milosevic on page 32 of the transcript of the 10th of April, 2003. Do you remember that? We can put it up on the screen if need be. But anyway, Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you had read the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and your answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. I remember very well the time I had in court with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you read at that time the role on the Federal Executive Council or, rather, the law on the Federal Executive Council, and the National Bank of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which was in force until 1992? Did you read those laws and regulations?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a number of questions relating to regulations. The law on the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia after the constitution was enacted, did you read that? And I'm referring in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: In general I can state that as of today, I cannot remember which laws I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you read the laws provided to you by someone from the Prosecutor, or did you request the OTP to provide you with certain laws and regulations that you considered would be necessary for you to be able to carry out your work? Do you remember that in methodological terms, I'm asking you now?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I can't remember which laws I requested or which laws were provided me now, six years later. No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that you know that in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as in Republika Srpska and the Serbian Republic of Krajina, who passed the budget.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yeah, it would be the government who had proposed the budget, and then it would be the Assembly would vote on the budget and pass the budget as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know -- did you read this in any of the regulations or come across a document which indicates who within the government proposed part of the budget earmarked for defence?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I told you that it was the Minister of Defence together with the Minister of Finance, would that be logical?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That sounds very logical, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the beneficiary of the defence budget? To be very specific, the budget of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia earmarked for defence, who was the beneficiary of that particular segment of the budget?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That would be the army, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Well, if we're talking about the army, it would be the officers employed in the army. It would be the soldiers, conscripts, all other personnel that was attached to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you claim that the part of the budget earmarked for defence was earmarked specifically for the army and whatever was within the army.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have another couple of questions in regard of methodology. Today, I understood that in preparing to compile this report, you made use of a large number of documents that you were provided by the OTP, and then you examined them or looked for the keyword, as you have described. Having been provided some of these documents by the assistants, you used these documents as a source for your own analysis.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I interpret this as classical analytical work. This was not investigative work. This was an analytical work on the basis of sources provided to you by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: It was very much an analytical job, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was at variance with what you had done before, where you actually investigated documents and sought out documents yourself. In this case you were offered these documents.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. To a certain extent that is correct. But also, all my previous jobs have been very much analytical, I mean, but the difference being here that I didn't initially collect the documents myself firsthand from the original source, that being the main difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In my view there is a methodological difference here, and I'm going to ask you whether I'm wrong. When you did your previous reports, when you worked on your previous jobs, when you were an investigator of these teams organised within the Norwegian bodies and some embezzlement of this is reported to you, so you come to an institution and the representatives of that institution provide you with some documents and then you ask them for something else, or you go to other institutions to find the solution which you're interested in; namely, you are not confined to just those documents given to you by this first company, but you also seek out some other sources yourself.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did seek out sources myself as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this report, when you prepared this paper, you worked exclusively on the basis of what was provided to you by the OTP, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Almost exclusively. Just to elaborate on that. For instance, the budgets that we have presented here today, these were not budgets that were entered into the evidence system of the OTP because -- so as such were not part of the OTP collected evidence, but they were still available in sort of the public domain of the OTP. But no one at the OTP had thought about this being of relevance before. So I requested these budgets to be presented to me and they were, and I reviewed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's have no mysteries. Budgets and budget revisions and final accounts are public documents in the public document -- in the public domain, both in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and in Republika Srpska, and all of them had been published in their respective Official Gazettes; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you have confirmed for us today that in your analysis, in 1994, you only examined for the fiscal year 1994 the budget of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That is correct. I asked the OTP to assist me in identifying the RS budget for 1994 and 1994 -- 1995, but I haven't received it, and it hasn't been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I found it only a couple of days ago myself, and it was quite simple to find. Did you ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe that last comment was really Mr. Lukic providing evidence, rather than a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My profound apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You knew, did you not, that those were public documents? Did you go to your colleagues from the OTP with whom you're working and tell them, I should like to be able to find all these budgets for Republika Srpska, for the Serbian Krajina, and for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and all the budget revisions and all the final accounts. This is what you certainly needed in your analysis, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it would have been helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But did you ask them to provide you with those documents?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I first asked them to identify them and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were you given such information? Could they identify them, or did they tell you that they could not identify them?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they looked for them but they couldn't identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had you been in your previous position, you would have had the power to go to a certain institution and ask for a specific document yourself. I mean when you were working as an investigator in the Norwegian organisation.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in the Republic of Srpska, a law had been passed on the Social Accountancy Service or the -- actually, you talked about the Public Accounting Service and the Public Auditing Service, but the designations have been changed, but functionally and operational-wise, they are the same organisation. Do you know that this law was passed in Republika Srpska in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I may have seen this law but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that under Article 8 of that law it has been envisaged that all documents and books of the Public Accounting Service of Republika Srpska are public documents, do you think that it would have been of assistance to you if you had examined the books of the Public Accounting Service of Republika Srpska in the period under review, namely, in the period in which you were doing your own investigations?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: That would have been of interest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you propose to the OTP at any point during your investigative and analytical work, namely, whilst examining all these documents, did you propose to the OTP to ask for a specific document from, for instance, the authorities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or in the Republika Srpska or in Croatia? Did you not think that that would help you locate, identify, a specific document, or did you not do so?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: We had -- we had several requests to the authorities in Belgrade and also, as far as I remember, other places. But I would just like to add to this because the situation at the OTP, I was the only financial investigator actually dealing with an enormous task, and if we were going to follow all angles regarding this case, it would have required a huge number of financial investigators or investigators with the right competence to follow up all the possible leads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But do you agree with me when I say that -- no, let me first ask you a layman's question from the legal aspect. Do you agree with me that it is always easy to follow the trail of money because there is always a trace left behind?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes. If it is recorded in proper records, it's always easy, and those records are made available. But if you are talking about following the trail of cash, that is not always easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your report you stated that financing of -- you claim that the financing of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina functioned via the Social Accounting Service, in which period it was actually derived from primary issue, that financing, that is.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that in such a situation if money is being printed in one institution and that money is being distributed somewhere via official state institutions, it is quite easy to follow the trail of such money. I'm not talking about cash.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: It should be at least, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Particularly so when these are public state institutions, the operation of which is regulated under a law which is a public document itself.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: It depends, again, on whether the law is followed or not and whether proper records are kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Prior to the beginning of your testimony, we had certain corrections in your paper which were conveyed to us by Colleague Saxon. I believe it is in paragraph 19, a sentence in paragraph 19. You said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the page with this paragraph could be called up on e-court so that Mr. Torkildsen could see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minute. It is page 19. It is coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the proofing notes compiled with you and the OTP in preparing you to appear before this Chamber, it was said that after the sentence "Slobodan Milosevic had no objections to money becoming accessible via primary issue," this is the sentence which you consider should be omitted from this report and should not be an integral part of it. Is my conclusion correct? Do you agree with me that you decided to change -- to change your report and this particular part after the cross-examination by Slobodan Milosevic and the argumentation which he adduced to you in connection with the discussions at that particular session of the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: From what I can recollect from my previous testimony, it's that Mr. Milosevic was arguing that he left at lunchtime during these discussions and therefore could not object, as I have made a point of in the report. So, yes, of course, if that was the case, I will have to go back on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But do you agree with me that at that particular session, he did not advocate primary issue. He was not in favour of it.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: What I'm stating here is that it's actually the result in the end. By looking at what happened later on, you see the consequences of the politics that was actually -- that was actually applied in the coming years. But in this particular session, I agree with you that he did not -- he did not say anything that he was specifically in favour of primary -- the use of primary emissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I correct when I say that now you have become more precise in respect of a specific matter which is not so stated in your report. This, again, emanates, in my view, from the examination in the Milosevic case, and that is when on transcript page 19044 you confirmed that there had been no primary emission any more as of January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Simply a concern. I'm sorry to interrupt. In the middle of that last question, again, my colleague said: "This, again, emanates in my view from the examination in the Milosevic case ..." and then the transcript page is mentioned. It just seems -- the record appears to be unclear whether we're hearing -- whether the evidence is Mr. Lukic's view or whether it's part of a question addressed to the witness. That's my only concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I'll be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'll be more precise. I have another question before you ask the next question. My question would then also be transcript page 19044, is this of the Milosevic trial? Do we have a copy of that page for the witness to see?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. We have inserted it in e-court. That is page 1D001548. That is the document. It is under that number that the document has been inserted into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I was just going to say that shouldn't we have disposed of P310, MFI, so that you can put it on the screen, but then I see that it has moved. Are you done with that previous document, Exhibit P310, MFI? You're done with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to use P310, MFI. I am going to use his work during my further interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see the relevant transcript. That's 19004.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 19044 is the official page of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is 1900, not 044.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I need is 044.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure the registrar is getting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Registry for not having called up the page properly, the way it should be done. It is the twentieth line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There you say -- you can read it. [In English] "Yes. I am aware that the inflation was stabilised in January 1994 when Governor Avramovic of the National Bank of Yugoslavia actually pegged the dinar to the Deutschemark." [Interpretation] And then the next page, Milosevic's question, and you respond in line 3: [In English] "... to finance budget deficit."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We cannot see line 3, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is: Since in your work you never referred to when the financing of Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska Krajina from the budget ended, you never say anything about that, do you agree with me that after examination by Milosevic you realised that this was an important matter which you should actually accentuate and also impress upon this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that if I had had the annual accounts or the budgets of the RS available for 1994 and 1995, that could have been of relevance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Without that particular fact you maintain the position, not having the budgets for 1994 and 1995, you maintain that the budget was no longer financed from primary issue after the introduction of this super-dinar, there was no more deficit financing, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: At least it wasn't -- to a very large extent, it was something like -- almost like 10 per cent a year. I have reviewed all the budgets for the FRY and the RSK for that period, and I do assume that the budgets of the RS would show the same picture for 1994 and 1995, as these other budgets that I have reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. You're saying, Mr. Torkildsen, you have reviewed all the budgets for the FRY and the RSK for that period, and you do assume that the budgets of the RS would show the same picture for 1994 and 1995 as these other budgets that you have reviewed. I thought a little earlier you had indicated that -- it actually was put to you that you didn't actually have access to the budgets for 1994 and 1995 for all these three entities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never seen the budgets for Republika Srpska, but I have seen some of the budgets for these other entities, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And on what basis would you then assume that the 1994/1995 budgets of the Republika Srpska which you didn't see would have had a 10 per cent allocation as the others had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that on the basis -- because of the previous year. The previous years showed the same pattern for all three entities. Either we're talking about the FRY, the RS, and the SRK, the method of financing was the same. So I then, as a result of that, assumed that that would also be the case for the RS, both for 1994 and for 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not basing it on maybe having had sight of the FRY budgets for 1994 and 1995 indicating a 10 per cent allocation towards the RSK, even -- towards RS, even if you did not see the RS budgets. You're not basing it on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the hyperinflation, the rate was in percentages when it was the highest, that is, towards the end of 1993, in the last months of 1993, in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: I know that it was extremely high, and I also made a table of that in the end of my report outlining this. We are talking here most likely a thousand per cent a day, or it could even be higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And just in a couple of sentences for the benefit of us in the courtroom understanding, what happened in January 1994? Who prepared this programme? And what was actually done at that particular moment? What was the point of that programme, its objective?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Its objective was to stop the inflation, and it was carried out under Governor Avramovic at the National Bank of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about him? I mean, have you formed a professional opinion on him?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether my question can stem from the response I've just been given, but do you know that in January 1994 he was appointed Governor of the National Bank of Yugoslavia and that is when he embarked upon this monetary reform of the monetary system in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interject, is the monetary reform of the monetary system of Yugoslavia the programme you're referring to in the previous question? I was going to ask you what is that programme you're talking about in -- if you look at page 92, from line 19 to 22, you're talking of a programme there, and you lost me. I'm not quite sure what programme you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to ask a few specific questions about this programme which is called the programme of the reconstruction of the monetary system and the financial stabilisation of the SFRY. Maybe I'm paraphrasing, but through the documents we'll be going back to that programme. But, Your Honours, if it is time now, because I will have another topic to broach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, indeed, time. Thank you very much. You have answered my question. Mr. Torkildsen, we haven't finished with you. It's time to adjourn for the day. You will have to come back tomorrow again at 9.00 in the morning. Let me just warn you that you may not talk to anybody about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar just reminded me that we don't sit tomorrow. We will sit on Monday. So you have to come back on Monday. Between now and then, you may not discuss this matter with anybody. Court adjourned to Monday, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Same courtroom at a quarter past 2.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of November, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
